sm: Todd Friel argues that false teaching promotes sin while good teaching promotes godliness, and begins a countdown of its consequences. He opens with a video of a self-styled African prophet, Rufus Fala, feeding a congregant an antiseptic not made for human consumption, as an obvious example of harm. Consequence number eight is that false doctrine confuses truth and error, making people gullible to the devil's lies. Number seven is that it prevents godliness, and he points to King Jeroboam in First Kings twelve, who built altars and made two golden calves so his people would not travel to Jerusalem. Number six is that false doctrine promotes sin, since Jeroboam sought the wisdom of man instead of reading his Bible.

Friel continues the story of Jeroboam, whose sin was so grievous that the wicked kings after him were described as committing it. Consequence five is that false doctrine elevates ungodly leadership, because congregations ignore the elder qualifications in First Timothy and Titus and accept a charismatic teacher who is a drunkard or womanizer. Four is that it permits false teachers, with billions of dollars given to them mostly by poor people, and the cure is a high view of Scripture. Three is that it removes God's blessing, and two is that it leaves the church unequipped for hardship, as with John Bunyan, who spent twelve years in prison rather than teach falsehood. One is that it weakens the future church, since each generation builds on the low teaching of the last. He closes with a comedy bit about a rich false teacher.
